# Opening: Christ had no biological father

**Thesis.** Christ's body came from Mary alone, by the Holy Ghost's act, with no man contributing. Joseph was his father only by supposition and by legal naming.

**Definition.** "Biological father" means a male parent from whom a child's flesh derives by natural generation, by a man "knowing" a woman. Everything below turns on that.

---

## 1. The direct statements of the conception

**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** *ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχουσα ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου* (*en gastri echousa ek pneumatos hagiou*) means "having in womb out of Spirit holy." The preposition *ἐκ* (*ek*, "out of") marks source or origin. The pregnancy is dated *πρὶν ἢ συνελθεῖν αὐτούς* (*prin ē synelthein autous*, "before they came together"), so Joseph is excluded by the text's own timeline.

**[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "But while he thought on these things, behold, the angel of the Lord appeared unto him in a dream, saying, Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** *τὸ ἐν αὐτῇ γεννηθὲν* (*to en autē gennēthen*) means "that which is begotten in her." Its source is again *ἐκ πνεύματός ἐστιν ἁγίου* (*ek pneumatos estin hagiou*, "out of Spirit it is holy"). Joseph's suspicion in Matthew 1:19, "minded to put her away privily," shows he knew the child was not his. The angel answers that suspicion by naming a different source.

**[L1] Luke 1:34-35:** "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man? And the angel answered and said unto her, The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω* (*andra ou ginōskō*) means "a man I do not know," using *γινώσκω* (*ginōskō*, "know") in its marital sense. The angel's answer gives no man at all. It gives *ἐπελεύσεται* (*epeleusetai*, "will come upon") and *ἐπισκιάσει* (*episkiasei*, "will overshadow"). The child is *ἐκ σοῦ* (*ek sou*, "out of you"), from Mary. The words *διὸ καί* (*dio kai*, "therefore also") make the sonship follow from this manner of conception.

**[L3]** Mary's question in Luke 1:34 only makes sense if ordinary generation was the expected path. The angel's reply supplies a different path.

---

## 2. Matthew's genealogy breaks its own pattern

**[L1] Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** Matthew 1:2-16 runs on *ἐγέννησεν* (*egennēsen*, "begat"), a man begetting a son. At the last link the verb changes to the passive *ἐγεννήθη* (*egennēthē*, "was born"). Its source is *ἐξ ἧς* (*ex hēs*, "out of whom"), a **feminine singular** relative pronoun, so it refers to Mary alone. Joseph is *ἄνδρα Μαρίας* (*andra Marias*, "husband of Mary"), not the one who begat.

**[L3]** This matches Matthew 1:25, "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son." The verb *ἐγίνωσκεν* (*eginōsken*, "was knowing") is negated through the conception and delivery.

---

## 3. Prophecy required it

**[L1] Isaiah 7:14:** "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

**[L2]** The Hebrew is *הָעַלְמָה* (*ha-almah*, "the young woman of marriageable age," with the definite article). The thing promised is *אוֹת* (*ʾôt*, "a sign"). Ordinary birth to a married woman is no sign.

**[L3]** Genesis 24:43 calls Rebekah *ha-almah*: "when the virgin cometh forth to draw water." Genesis 24:16 says of the same woman: "a virgin, neither had any man known her." There the Hebrew *בְּתוּלָה* (*bethulah*, "virgin") is explained by "neither had any man known her." The same person is called *almah* in one place and *bethulah* in the other, so *almah* can carry a virgin sense.

**[L1] Matthew 1:22-23:** "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying, Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us."

**[L2]** *παρθένος* (*parthenos*, "virgin") is Matthew's term. Luke 1:27 uses it of Mary: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph... and the virgin's name was Mary."

---

## 4. Other New Testament witnesses

**[L1] Galatians 4:4:** "But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law."

**[L2]** *γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός* (*genomenon ek gynaikos*) means "become out of a woman." Only the woman is named as the human source.

**[L3]** Genesis 3:15 says "her seed," using *זֶרַע* (*zera'*, "seed") of the woman, not of the man. Hebrews 10:5 says "a body hast thou prepared me."

**[L1] Luke 3:23:** "And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was the son of Heli."

**[L2]** *ὡς ἐνομίζετο* (*hōs enomizeto*, "as was supposed, as was thought") marks the common belief as an assumption, not a fact.

---

## 5. Objections answered

**"Thy father" in Luke 2:48.** [L1] Mary says "behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." [L1] Jesus replies in Luke 2:49, "wist ye not that I must be about my father's business?" Mary uses the household term, and Jesus immediately redirects the word "father." [L3] John 6:42 has the crowd saying "whose father and mother we know," and Matthew 13:55 has "the carpenter's son." These are public assumptions of the kind Luke 3:23 labels "as was supposed."

**"Seed of David" through Joseph.** [L1] Romans 1:3 says "made of the seed of David according to the flesh." [L2] *κατὰ σάρκα* (*kata sarka*, "according to flesh") places the Davidic descent in the flesh, which came from Mary. [L3] Luke 1:32 says "the throne of his father David," where "father" means ancestor, so "father" in Scripture does not always mean biological parent. [L3] Joseph's naming in Matthew 1:21 and 1:25 ("he called his name JESUS") gives Jesus his legal place in the house of David. [L4] The Davidic flesh through Mary and the legal right through Joseph both fit these verses without a biological father. Luke 1:32 and Romans 1:3 supply the two footings, and the chain runs from "flesh" to Mary and from "naming" to Joseph.

**"The Holy Ghost as biological father."** [L4] The text does not describe generation by "knowing." Luke 1:34 rules out a man, and Luke 1:35 uses *overshadow* and *power*, the language of creative act. Matthew 1:20's *ek pneumatos* is origin of the conception, not the paternity of a male parent supplying seed. Hebrews 10:5 describes the body as *prepared*, which is the language of making. The footings are Luke 1:34-35 [L1], the *ek* and *episkiasei* usage [L2], and Hebrews 10:5 [L3].

---

## DECLARED CHAIN -- the links your case stands on

1. Mary's pregnancy is dated before she and Joseph "came together" and is sourced "of the Holy Ghost." Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:18 and 1:20; [L2] *ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου* (*ek pneumatos hagiou*, "out of Spirit holy"), where *ek* marks origin, and *πρὶν ἢ συνελθεῖν* (*prin ē synelthein*, "before they came together").
2. Mary explicitly excludes a man, and the angel names a non-marital mode of conception. Footing: [L1] Luke 1:34-35 "I know not a man... The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee"; [L2] *ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω* (*andra ou ginōskō*, "a man I do not know"), *ἐπισκιάσει* (*episkiasei*, "will overshadow"), and *ἐκ σοῦ* (*ek sou*, "out of you"); [L3] Matthew 1:25 "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
3. Matthew 1:16 breaks the "begat" pattern and sources Jesus from Mary alone. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:16; [L2] *ἐγεννήθη* (*egennēthē*, "was born") with the feminine *ἐξ ἧς* (*ex hēs*, "out of whom"); [L3] contrast with the repeated *ἐγέννησεν* (*egennēsen*, "begat") of Matthew 1:2-15.
4. Isaiah 7:14 promised a sign of conception by a virgin, and Matthew applies it to Mary. Footing: [L1] Isaiah 7:14 and Matthew 1:22-23; [L2] *ha-almah* and *ʾôt* (a sign), with *παρθένος* (*parthenos*, "virgin"); [L3] Genesis 24:43 with Genesis 24:16 ("neither had any man known her") shows *almah* can describe a virgin.
5. Joseph's fatherhood is by supposition and law, not by generation. Footing: [L1] Luke 3:23 "as was supposed" and Luke 2:48-49; [L2] *ὡς ἐνομίζετο* (*hōs enomizeto*, "as was supposed"); [L3] Luke 1:32 "his father David" and Matthew 1:21, 1:25 (the naming) show "father" can be ancestral or legal.
6. Christ had no biological father: his flesh came from Mary alone by the Holy Ghost's act, and Joseph was only his supposed and legal father. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:18-25, Luke 1:34-35, Galatians 4:4; [L2] *ek* ("out of") of origin, *ex hēs* (feminine "out of whom"), *ek gynaikos* ("out of a woman"); [L3] Isaiah 7:14 with Matthew 1:23, Genesis 3:15, and Hebrews 10:5.

# Round 2: Defense of D1-D6

**Framing.** The case is a chain: conception sourced in the Holy Ghost, no man in the marital window, the genealogy's pattern withheld from Joseph, the sign promised, and Joseph's fatherhood marked as supposed. The challenger has taken the links one at a time and read each in isolation. A term cut from its chain proves nothing, so I re-seat each one.

---

## I. The seed rows (Romans 1:3, Acts 2:30, 2 Samuel 7:12, Psalm 132:11, Hebrews 7:14, 2 Timothy 2:8)

**1. The verb in Romans 1:3 is the verb of Galatians 4:4.**
- [L1] Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh." [L1] Galatians 4:4: "made of a woman."
- [L2] Romans 1:3 reads *τοῦ γενομένου ἐκ σπέρματος Δαυίδ* (*tou genomenou ek spermatos David*, "who became out of seed of David"). Galatians 4:4 reads *γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός* (*genomenon ek gynaikos*, "become out of a woman").
- Both use *γίνομαι* (*ginomai*, "to become, be made") with *ἐκ* (*ek*, "out of"). Neither uses *γεννάω* (*gennaō*, "to beget"), the verb Matthew uses for a man begetting.
- [L4] The one Son is "made of the seed of David" and "made of a woman" by the same verb and preposition. The woman is therefore the channel of the Davidic seed. This rests on Romans 1:3 [L1/L2] and Galatians 4:4 [L1/L2]. The challenger's rows say what Christ descended from. They do not say a man begat him.

**2. "Seed" is not the man's alone.**
- The challenger's [L2] gloss, "the man's seed, as of a sower," is contradicted at the Hebrew word.
- [L1] Genesis 3:15: "between thy seed and her seed." [L1] Genesis 16:10, to Hagar: "I will multiply thy seed exceedingly." [L1] Genesis 24:60, to Rebekah: "let thy seed possess the gate of those which hate them."
- [L2] *זֶרַע* (*zera'*, "seed") is said of women three times. [L3] The KJV's own usage refutes the claim that "seed" needs a male last link.

**3. "Loins" and "bowels" name descent.**
- [L1] Hebrews 7:10: Levi "was yet in the loins of his father, when Melchisedec met him." Levi was in Abraham's loins through generations and through the mothers of those generations.
- [L2] *ὀσφύς* (*osphys*, "loins") and, in 2 Samuel 7:12, *מֵעֶיךָ* (*me'ekha*, "thy bowels") mark lineage at any depth. They do not name the last begetter.
- Acts 2:30 and Psalm 132:11 are covenant oaths about David's line. They do not state how the last link was formed.

**4. Mary and David.**
- No verse is needed that gives a genealogy of Mary. The chain needs the verb and preposition of point 1, and Luke 1:32 [L1], spoken to Mary: "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David."
- The challenger's Aaron objection runs one way only. [L1] Luke 1:36 calls Elisabeth Mary's "cousin," which does not say Mary is of Levi.
- [L3] Exodus 6:23: "And Aaron took him Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Naashon." [L3] Numbers 2:3: "Nahshon the son of Amminadab shall be captain of the children of Judah." Aaron's line married into Judah's, so kinship with Elisabeth does not exclude Judah.
- [L4] This rests on Luke 1:36 [L1] and on Exodus 6:23 with Numbers 2:3 [L3].

**5. Legal reckoning.**
- Numbers 1:2 is a census instruction. It is not a rule about conception.
- [L3] Ezra 2:61 shows a man who "took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called after their name." Israel recognised naming into a house by marriage and law.
- That is the footing of D5: Joseph's naming (Matthew 1:21, 1:25) gives the legal place. The seed rows and legal reckoning fit a child with no human father, provided Joseph's fatherhood is legal.

---

## II. D1: Matthew 1:18 and 1:25

- [L1] Matthew 1:18: "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost." [L1] Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
- The challenger concedes the second row: *ἕως οὗ* (*heōs hou*, "until which") bounds the not-knowing through the pregnancy to the delivery.
- Then every point where Joseph could have known her is closed:
  - Before the pregnancy was found, they had not "come together" (1:18).
  - From the taking of his wife (1:24) to the delivery, he "knew her not" (1:25).
  - Mary says "I know not a man" (Luke 1:34).
- [L4] The challenger's reading needs a window that no verse supplies. This rests on Matthew 1:18 [L1], Matthew 1:25 [L1] with *ἐγίνωσκεν* (*eginōsken*, "was knowing," imperfect, negated), and Luke 1:34 [L1/L2].
- [L1] Genesis 4:1, "Adam knew Eve his wife: and she conceived," is the canon's ordinary means. That is exactly what Matthew 1:25 and Luke 1:34 deny at the points where it would apply.
- On 1 Corinthians 7:5, *συνέρχομαι* (*synerchomai*, "come together") can name marital union. The verb names the event whose absence Matthew 1:18 dates before the finding.

**Matthew 1:19-20.**
- The verse gives no verb of knowledge, but verse 20 answers the thought.
- [L1] "But while he thought on these things... Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
- [L2] *γάρ* (*gar*, "for") gives the reason for "fear not": the source of the conception.
- [L4] An angel does not remove fear by naming a source unless the source was the matter in doubt. If Joseph were the source, neither the putting away nor the reply would make sense. This rests on Matthew 1:19-20 [L1] and on *gar* [L2].

---

## III. D2: Luke 1:34-35

**The question.**
- [L1] Luke 1:27 says Mary is espoused. [L1] Luke 1:31 says "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son."
- If Joseph's coming marriage were the means, "How shall this be?" would have an obvious answer, so the question would not arise.
- The angel's answer names a different agent: [L1] "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee."
- The present tense of *ginōskō* gives her state at that time. It does not need to be permanent. The angel's reply to her question names no man.

**The verbs.**
- The challenger says *epeleusetai* and *episkiasei* never denote begetting. That treats the verbs apart from their clause.
- [L1] Luke 1:35 gives the result in the same sentence: "therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee."
- [L2] *διό* (*dio*, "wherefore") plus *καί* (*kai*, "also") makes the sonship a consequence of the coming and overshadowing.
- [L4] This rests on Luke 1:35 [L1] and on *dio kai* [L2].

**Sonship.**
- [L1] Luke 1:32 gives "Son of the Highest" before the question, but Luke 1:35 gives it again with a stated ground.
- [L1] 2 Samuel 7:14 and 1 Chronicles 28:6 say of Solomon "I will be his father." They never say "therefore" from his conception. Luke 1:35 does.
- [L3] Luke 1:36-37 pairs the sign of Elisabeth's conceiving in old age with "For with God nothing shall be impossible." The pairing marks Mary's conception as the greater work, not the ordinary one.

---

## IV. D3: Matthew 1:16

- The challenger says silence is not denial. The point is not one silence but a pattern in the chain.
- [L1] Matthew 1:3: "Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar." [L1] Matthew 1:5: "Salmon begat Booz of Rachab; and Booz begat Obed of Ruth." [L1] Matthew 1:6: "David the king begat Solomon of her that had been the wife of Urias."
- [L2] Each time a woman is named with *ἐκ* (*ek*, "out of") and a man is the subject of *ἐγέννησεν* (*egennēsen*, "begat").
- At 1:16 the woman is named with the feminine *ἐξ ἧς* (*ex hēs*, "out of whom"), but Joseph is *ἀνήρ* (*anēr*, "husband"), not the subject of "begat."
- [L4] The challenger says the feminine is expected because Mary bore the child. That is true in verses 3, 5 and 6 as well, but there the man is the begetter. Only at verse 16 is the active verb withheld. This rests on Matthew 1:3-6 and 1:16 [L1] and on the *ek/ex hēs* with *egennēsen* contrast [L2], and Matthew 1:20 supplies the stated reason.
- [L2] In Matthew 1:20 *γεννηθέν* (*gennēthen*, "begotten") is itself the begetting verb. Its source is *ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου* (*ek pneumatos hagiou*, "out of the Holy Spirit"). So Matthew speaks of begetting, and names the Spirit.

---

## V. D4: Isaiah 7:14

- [L1] Isaiah 7:11 sets the standard: "Ask thee a sign of the LORD thy God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above." Verse 14 answers: "the Lord himself shall give you a sign."
- [L2] *אוֹת* (*ʾôt*, "a sign") is measured against "depth" and "height." [L4] An ordinary birth does not match that standard. This rests on Isaiah 7:11 and 7:14 [L1] and on *ʾôt* [L2].
- On *almah*, the KJV itself renders the plural of this word "virgins" at [L1] Song of Solomon 1:3, "therefore do the virgins love thee." [L3] With Genesis 24:43 (Rebekah) and Genesis 24:16 ("neither had any man known her"), no occurrence names a married woman.
- On *bethulah*: [L1] Joel 1:8, "Lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth," shows that word also covers a woman with a husband. Its absence in Isaiah 7:14 proves nothing.
- [L1] Matthew 1:22-23 is inspired application: "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled." The Greek is *παρθένος* (*parthenos*, "virgin"), and the challenger has not answered Matthew's own word.
- On Isaiah 7:16 and 8:8, a prophecy can have a near horizon. [L3] Isaiah 9:6-7 speaks of "a child... born" with "his name... The mighty God," on "the throne of David." This is the same child at a larger horizon.

---

## VI. Galatians 4:4, Hebrews 10:5, Luke 3:23, Luke 2

**Galatians 4:4 and the Job idiom.**
- The idiom covers mortality, and that is not in dispute. But Paul writes "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman," with the sender named and the human source named, and no man.
- [L3] Genesis 3:15 ("her seed") and point 2 above show Scripture speaks of the woman's seed.

**Hebrews 10:5.**
- [L1] "a body hast thou prepared me." [L2] *κατηρτίσω* (*katērtisō*, "thou hast fitted, prepared"). [L3] Hebrews 11:3: "the worlds were framed by the word of God." *καταρτίζω* (*katartizō*, "to fit, frame") is the same verb, used there of God's making.
- [L4] The body is God's work, as the worlds are. This rests on Hebrews 10:5 [L1/L2] and on Hebrews 11:3 [L3].

**D5 and the four registers.**
- The challenger quotes Luke 2:48, Luke 2:27 and 2:41, John 6:42, John 1:45 and Luke 4:22. Those are speakers' words and household usage.
- The narrator himself writes [L1] Luke 2:33: "Joseph and his mother marvelled," not "his father and mother."
- [L1] Luke 2:49 is unanswered: "wist ye not that I must be about my father's business?" Jesus redirects "father" at once.
- On *ἐνομίζετο* (*enomizeto*, "was supposed"): context decides, as the challenger says. In Luke 3:23 the context is *ὡς* (*hōs*, "as") plus the parenthesis. [L4] A narrator who has just written Luke 1:34-35 would not hedge Joseph's fatherhood in a parenthesis if Joseph were the begetter. This rests on Luke 3:23 [L1/L2] and Luke 1:34-35 [L1].
- [L1] Luke 1:27 had already put Joseph on the family side: "a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David."

---

## Chain status

Each link has been re-seated in its chain: the Spirit as source, no marital window, the genealogy pattern broken, the sign promised, and Joseph's fatherhood supposed and legal. Every [L4] above exhibits at least two footings. The challenger's seed, loins and covenant-title rows state descent and covenant sonship. None states that a man begat Christ.

## D5 — "Joseph's fatherhood is by supposition and law, not by generation"

The text names Joseph as father in four registers, not one:

**A disciple:** "Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph" (John 1:45).

**The angel:** "Joseph, thou son of David" (Matthew 1:20).

The defender dismisses these as "public assumptions." But [L2] ἐνομίζετο (*enomizeto*, "was supposed / was wont") carries no verdict of its own — the same verb form is "where prayer was wont to be made" (Acts 16:13). Each context decides. Luke 3:23 stands in the same gospel with Mary's "thy father" (Luke 2:48) and the narrator's "his parents" (Luke 2:27, 41). **D5 is broken.**

The defender reads Matthew 1:19 as Joseph "knew the child was not his." At the word level the verse says: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily." [L2] δίκαιος ὤν (*dikaios ōn*, "being just"), μὴ θέλων αὐτὴν παραδειγματῖσαι (*mē thelōn autēn paradeigmatisai*, "not willing her to make a public example") — intent and two grounds.
